corrected_value.title: Power and overconﬁdent decision-making.

decision.location: Introduction specific empirical prediction, Methods and Results; independently verified primary author abstract0199
decision.quote:
Building from these ﬁndings, Fast and colleagues (2012)
reported ﬁve experiments that used multiple instantiations of power – including manip-
ulations via episodic recall tasks, role assignment, and extant work related power –
where they found high power to be associated with overconﬁdent decision-making.
Based on these ﬁndings, we propose that exaggerated expressions of conﬁdence will
emerge as a function of the degree to which high-power poses facilitate a high-power
mind-set.
decision.reason: The current report explicitly attributes a power-to-overconfident-decision relationship to Fast2012and predicts that inducing a high-power mindset through postures will produce greater overconfidence. It measures calibrated general-knowledge confidence before/after posing and directly tests the high/low-posture comparison on new108participants. The independently recovered primary author abstract verifies five empirical power/overconfidence experiments and the subjective-power condition. This is a designed conceptual retest of that published association within a new mediation design; novelty of the testosterone pathway does not turn the separately tested power-overconfidence link into background. Failure of the current felt-power manipulation affects interpretation/outcome, not the fact that the empirical link was tested. Full original task/scoring details remain unavailable after recorded attempts; no exact task or sample equivalence is asserted. Existing1047Carney2010reports posture/hormone/risk effects without the Fastoverconfidence experiments; it cannot represent this independent original. Different year/DOI alone is not the distinction. No outcome is requested or inferred.

corrected_value.authors: Mehta, P. H., Welker, K. M., Zilioli, S., & Carré, J. M.
corrected_value.title: Testosterone and cortisol jointly modulate risk-taking.

decision.location: Introduction specific empirical prediction, Methods and Results; independently verified primary author abstract0199
decision.quote:
Alternatively, the relationship
between embodied power and risk-taking may be jointly mediated by the interaction
between testosterone and cortisol. Mehta and Josephs (2010) have proposed a “dual
hormone hypothesis,” whereby cortisol modulates the eﬀect of testosterone on beha-
vior, such as risk-taking (Mehta, Welker, Zilioli, & Carré, 2015). Because Carney et al.
(2010) found high-power poses to both increase testosterone and decrease cortisol, the
interaction between these eﬀects may predict risk-taking, as has been previously shown
(Mehta et al., 2015). Furthermore, although Ranehill et al. (2015) failed to replicate
Carney et al.’s (2010) eﬀects of power posing on hormonal changes, other manipulations
related to power, such as winning a competition, have been shown to jointly impact
testosterone and cortisol (e.g. see Hamilton, Carré, Mehta, Olmstead, & Whitaker, 2015).
Thus, in the present research, we measured both testosterone and cortisol at two time
points, as per Carney et al.’s (2010) original design and tested for both main and
interactive eﬀects.
decision.reason: The current report explicitly invokes Mehta2015as the previous empirical testosterone-by-cortisol prediction of risk-taking, promises an interaction test, and tests that interaction against new participants gambling decisions. The independently recovered primary abstract verifies the conditional positive basal-testosterone/risk association at low rather than high basal cortisol in two studies. Current T2post-manipulation concentrations and a binary gamble differ from the original basal sampling and risk instruments; they must not be relabelled as basal measurements or hormone change-score interactions. Those differences qualify construct correspondence but do not erase the expressly intended conceptual test of the conditional hormone-risk association. The untested/new causal mediation proposal is distinguished from the interaction actually evaluated. Full original Methods and participant overlap remain unknown after attempts; exact protocol or causal equivalence is not asserted. Existing1047Carney2010does not report these two Mehta dual-hormone moderation studies. This is an absent empirical original, not a new row inferred only from a distinct DOI. No outcome is assigned.

Our results provide evidence that this is not due to a null effect of reward on memory, because both here and in our previous experiment reward increased memory recall robustly. Replicating much previous work, when high- and low-reward items were studied and tested together, reward increased recall. We observed this effect both in the immediate test and in the delayed test. Replicating our own and other previous studies (Nilsson 1987; Ngaosuvan and Mantila 2005; experiment 1 in Stefanidi et al. 2018; Talmi et al. 2021), reward did not increase recall in pure lists. We observed that in the immediate test of pure lists, reward actually decreased recall here, a finding we have not observed before and that would require replication. The average performance in the delayed recall test here was better than in our previous study, providing reassurance that our previous finding of a null effect of reward on forgetting in cued free recall was not due to floor effects.
